query: For high-entropy alloys in demanding engineering applications, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve resistance to thermally induced toughness loss, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, defines the conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment that could falsify it?

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of refractory elements in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) can improve their resistance to thermally induced toughness loss.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase HEAs with a face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) structure
generation.intervention: Addition of refractory elements such as W, Mo, Ta, Nb, Hf, etc. in equi- or near equi-molar ratios
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable solid solution or precipitation of a secondary phase
generation.mechanism: Solid solution strengthening or precipitation strengthening mechanism, where the refractory elements or secondary phase hinders dislocation movement and improves toughness
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved resistance to thermally induced toughness loss, resulting in enhanced high-temperature mechanical properties
generation.baseline: Single-phase HEAs without the refractory elements
generation.uncertainty: The stability and coherence of the solid solution or secondary phase may be affected by the specific alloy composition and processing conditions

falsification_experiment.design: High-temperature mechanical testing of HEAs with and without the refractory elements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEAs with the refractory elements do not show improved resistance to thermally induced toughness loss, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

In the last few decades, the development of nickel-based superalloys has allowed a steady increase in operating temperatures of jet turbine engines, which leads to enhanced engine performance and efficiency. However, nowadays the engine operating temperatures have reached around 80% of the melting points of the materials, [1] i.e. , almost reaching the upper limit of usability, making it impossible to further increase the operating temperature. Thus, it is urgently needed to develop new materials that can withstand higher operating temperatures to achieve better performance, higher engine efficiency, and lower greenhouse gas emissions.

Among various potential candidates, such as ceramics, [3] intermetallic compounds, [6] and refractory metals, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [8] have drawn considerable attention in the past decade because of their very encouraging properties, for instance, high melting points, superior mechanical properties at both room temperature and elevated temperatures, [13] which makes RHEAs of great interest for high-temperature application.
